query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In pre-passivated Q235 steel, the protective behavior under corrosive exposure is governed by the stability of the initially formed passivation film: at room temperature, the dense passivated layer retards corrosion via its electrochemical barrier properties, whereas at high temperatures (700–900 °C) thermal stresses induce phase transformations and microcracking in the film that compromise its integrity, leading to accelerated corrosion. In some cases, if a self-healing mixed oxide scale (rich in more stable Fe3+ compounds) forms, it may locally restore protection, but only if the film’s microstructure is able to re-establish continuity despite high thermal cycling.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 low-carbon steel in its pre-exposure state after pickling and passivation treatment with a uniform, dense dark passivation film.
generation.intervention: Expose identical pre-passivated Q235 specimens to a controlled cyclic salt spray environment at room temperature and to a simulated high-temperature (700–900 °C) salt exposure regime.
generation.conditions: For group A: cyclic salt spray tests under ambient temperature (humid atmospheric corrosion) conditions. For group B: controlled high-temperature salt exposure using a furnace (with appropriate salt deposits) to simulate boiler-like conditions, ensuring comparable salt concentration and exposure duration.
generation.structural_mediator: The microstructural integrity and phase composition of the passivation film, including the size and connectivity of any microcracks and the nature of the iron oxide phases present.
generation.mechanism: At ambient conditions, the passivation film acts as an effective electrochemical barrier, limiting ionic transport and corrosion. Under high-temperature exposure, thermal stresses promote phase transformations (e.g., from FeO to more brittle Fe2O3/Fe3O4) and microcrack development, which increase chloride ion ingress and disrupt the continuous barrier; any observed stabilization would be due to a self-healing process forming a denser, adherent mixed oxide layer.
generation.predicted_outcome: Room-temperature specimens will show slower, more uniform corrosion with modest weight loss and limited localized pitting. In contrast, high-temperature specimens will exhibit more pronounced microcracking, phase changes in the passivation film, and accelerated, localized corrosion (with higher weight loss and more extensive pit formation) unless a resilient self-healed oxide layer emerges, in which case the degradation may be partially arrested.
generation.baseline: The corrosion behavior of passivated Q235 steel under room-temperature cyclic salt spray exposure, where the original passivation film provides sustained protection, serves as the baseline.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies specifically to Q235 steel in its pre-passivated state under salt-rich atmospheric and high-temperature exposures. It may not hold for Q235 with additional alloying modifications or applied metal/alloy coatings that have inherently different high-temperature or corrosion behaviors.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal combines observations of passivation film breakdown and weight loss trends in atmospheric salt spray tests (e.g., evidence from PMC9504384 :: web ::028 :: 4_conclusions) with temperature‐driven changes in passivation film growth and composition (e.g., evidence from PMC9867134 :: web ::000 :: abstract). It remains uncertain how well the in‐lab high-temperature conditions replicate real service cycles and whether self-healing oxide formation can consistently offset film degradation under dynamic thermal stresses.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of pre-passivated Q235 steel specimens (using the identical pickling and passivation process). Divide them into two groups: one group will undergo standard cyclic salt spray exposure at room temperature, and the other will be subjected to cyclic high-temperature salt exposure (700–900 °C) in a furnace with controlled thermal cycles that mimic boiler conditions. Monitor both groups over identical cumulative exposure times.
measurements: Weight loss measurements to determine corrosion rate.
SEM imaging to observe microstructural integrity and development of cracks in the passivation film.
XPS/EDS analysis to identify phase changes and oxide compositions in the protective film.
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to evaluate the barrier properties of the film before and after exposure.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high-temperature exposure does not lead to statistically significant deterioration in film integrity (e.g., no increased microcrack density, similar oxide composition, or comparable weight loss and corrosion rates as room-temperature specimens) or if a self-healing oxide scale forms with similar protective properties as the original passivation film, the proposed mechanism (that thermal stresses compromise the film and accelerate corrosion) would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, the corrosion behavior and mechanism of Q235 in atmospheric environment are studied by designing a cyclic salt spray accelerated corrosion experiment. The specific conclusions are as follows: Q235 low-carbon steel in the atmospheric environment of the accelerated corrosion process can be roughly divided into four stages: (1) passivation film corrosion product generation and local shedding, (2) matrix rust layer generation and covering, (3) rust layer accumulation and stacking onto a flat and dense second protective layer, and (4) matrix rust layer breaking through the protective layer continues to grow thicker until shedding. After pickling passivation treatment of Q235 low-carbon steel in the atmospheric environment of corrosion from passivation film weakness, pitting corrosion gradually develops into comprehensive corrosion with the elongation of time. Rust layer composition gradually transitions from passivation products into iron oxide based on hydroxyl iron oxide. The whole process is “from point to surface” corrosion. Concrete, especially mass concrete, releases a large amount of heat during the hydration process, resulting in the passivation of reinforcement at high temperatures. However, the passivation study of reinforced concrete is mostly conducted at room temperature, and the influence of temperature on passive film behavior is not clear at present. The passivation film of reinforcing steel directly determines the corrosion resistance of reinforcing steel and affects the service life of reinforced concrete. Herein, the passivation of Q235 steel soaking in simulated concrete pore (SCP) solution at 20 °C, 40 °C, and 60 °C is explored. It is found that the passivation process is divided into two stages, with 24 h as the boundary; within 24 h the passivation was carried out rapidly, and the passive film is in a relatively stable state after 24 h. In addition, the higher the temperature, the faster the passivation. Moreover, under the condition of higher temperatures, more Fe3+ compounds are produced, and the semiconductor properties of passivated films are more stable. Based on experiments, the passivation mechanism affected by temperature was analyzed in detail.
